newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Stubborn NZ inflation prods rates, currency higher.
newsitem.headline: Stubborn NZ inflation prods rates, currency higher.

text.p: Worse than expected inflation figures put paid to hopes of further interest rate falls and pushed the New Zealand dollar higher on Friday.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.7 percent in the December quarter against economists' expectations of 0.36 percent, while underlying inflation came in at 0.63 percent for the quarter and 2.4 per cent for the year.
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand had forecast quarterly underlying inflation of 0.5 percent, while economists were predicting 0.4.
A new centre-right coalition government last month gave the central bank more room to manoeuvre by relaxing its underlying inflation target to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent.
But economists said the annual rate was well above the mid-point of the target range, allowing no room for complacency.
"That means that the RBNZ is going to remain reasonably vigilant," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
"It certainly...does put any thought of easing into the background for some time now," said Matthew Goodson, economist at sharebrokers Garlick and Co.
Housing costs were the main contributor to the CPI rise, but other factors included higher air fares, health insurance, local authority rates and more expensive clothing.
The data surprised financial markets, which had been braced to push interest rates and the currency lower if inflation came in below forecasts.

The New Zealand dollar initially shot above US$0.71 after opening just above 0.7060, but settled back in afternoon trade to just below 0.7090. Short-term interest rates rose five points from Thursday's close to 7.48 percent, while bond yields also climbed.
The Trade-Weighted Index, which measures the Kiwi dollar against a basket of currencies, surged above 68.5 to hit its highest levels since late 1987.
Its rise spells pain for exporters, manufacturers and farmers who have long called for a weaker dollar to make their goods more competitive.

"The latest figures show, yet again, that the present balance of monetary and economic policy is not able to deliver price stability without a seriously over-valued exchange rate," opposition Labour party finance spokesman Michael Cullen said.

The Kiwi's latest rise presents a headache for Winston Peters, leader of the New Zealand First party and Treasurer in the new coalition government. Peters said repeatedly during last year's election campaign that he intended to drive the New Zealand dollar down.
Foreign exchange dealers said the Kiwi was far higher than the RBNZ wanted, but the bank was powerless to control the mix of currency and interest rate conditions.

"I think further down the track, the prospect of a weaker economy may well be the thing that triggers a lower currency and lower rates, but that's not going to happen in the near-term," said Chris Rand, chief forex manager at Westpac.
